title: II. God's nature viewed in essence and persons — Cap. 5 close
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): II. Ye nature belonging toward God in essence plus persons is viewed. Knowledge belonging toward ye one essence from ye book belonging toward nature plus belonging toward Scripture jointly is sought: knowledge belonging toward ye three distinct persons from ye book belonging toward Scripture alone. That ye name belonging toward essence truly unto God belongs from this we understand, that He ye first plus highest being is, on whom all other beings depend. But if being He is, certainly essence He has: since by it being necessarily is defined. And because God essence from Himself has plus not from elsewhere, plus therefore perpetually possesses it, also essence in ye abstract He is said to be: from which Jerome (tome 2, letter unto Damasus): One, he says, plus only nature belonging toward God, which truly is. For that which subsists does not have from elsewhere, but its own is. Ye rest which created are, even if to be they seem, are not, because once they were not, plus again not be what they were they can. God alone, who eternal is — that is, who no beginning has — ye name belonging toward essence truly holds. Concerning ye name belonging toward ye persons from Scripture (1 John 5:7; Hebrews 1:3) more inwardly it will be seen.
pass_b_english: II. The nature of God is viewed in essence and persons. Knowledge of the one essence is sought from the book of nature and of Scripture jointly: knowledge of the three distinct persons from the book of Scripture alone.

That the name of essence truly belongs to God we understand from this, that He is the first and highest being, on whom all other beings depend. But if He is being, He certainly has essence: since by it being is necessarily defined. And because God has essence from Himself and not from elsewhere, and therefore possesses it perpetually, He is also said to be essence in the abstract: from which Jerome (tome 2, letter to Damasus): One, he says, and only nature of God, which truly is. For that which subsists does not have from elsewhere, but is its own. The rest which are created, even if they seem to be, are not, because once they were not, and can again not be what they were. God alone, who is eternal — that is, who has no beginning — truly holds the name of essence.
Concerning the name of the persons from Scripture (1 John 5:7; Hebrews 1:3) it will be seen more inwardly.
source_text: II. Natura Dei spectatur in essentia & personis. Cognitio unius essentiae petitur e libro naturae & scripturae conjunctim: cognitio trium distinctarum personarum ex libro scripturae tantum. Essentiae nomen vere Deo convenire, ex hoc intelligimus, quod is est ens primum & summum, a quo caetera entia omnia dependent. Si vero ens est, utique habet essentiam: cum per eam ens necessario definiatur. Et, quia Deus essentiam a seipso habet, & non aliunde; ideoque eam perpetuo possidet; in abstracto quoque essentia esse dicitur: unde Hieronymus tom. 2. epistola ad Damasum: Una, inquit, Dei & sola natura, quae vere est. Id enim, quod subsistít, non habet aliunde, sed suum est. Caetera, quae creata sunt, etiamsi videntur esse, non sunt, quia aliquando non fuerunt, & possunt rursum non esse quod fuerunt. Deus solus, qui aeternus est, hoc est, qui exordium non habet, essentiae nomen vere tenet. De nomine personarum e scriptura 1 Joh. 5.7; Heb. 1.3. interius videbitur.
